title: Places: à, en, au, chez
description: Say where you are, where you go and where you come from.

guide.summary: This topic gives you the little words that place people and things: where you live, where you are going, where you come from, and what is next to what.

sections.title: In or to a city or a country?
sections.text: French uses one word for both in and to: J’habite à Lyon and Je vais à Lyon. What you must choose depends on the place, not on the verb.

rows: à Paris, à Tokyo, à Rome
en France, en Espagne, en Allemagne
en Europe, en Asie, en Afrique
en Iran, en Israël, en Angola
au Canada, au Japon, au Brésil

steps: Decide what the place is: a city, a country, or a continent.
For a country, find its article: la, le or les.
Take the row that matches, and remember that a vowel at the start of a country beats its gender.

examples.en: I live in Lyon, in France.

examples.fr: Ils partent au Canada en juin.
examples.en: They are leaving for Canada in June.

examples.fr: Tu vas aux États-Unis cet été ?
examples.en: Are you going to the United States this summer?

watch: Cities take no article: never au Paris, never en Madrid.
à carries a grave accent; a with no accent is the verb avoir.
à le is never written: à + le becomes au, à + les becomes aux.

sections.title: Is the country masculine, feminine or plural?
sections.text: Learn the country with its article, the way you learn a noun. Most countries ending in -e are feminine, but a few are masculine, such as le Mexique and le Cambodge.
steps: Say the country with its article to yourself: la Suisse, le Portugal, les Philippines.
Ending in -e usually means feminine, but check the known exceptions.
If the name starts with a vowel, the gender stops mattering for in and to.

examples.fr: Le Mexique est un beau pays.

watch: Le Mexique ends in -e but is masculine: au Mexique, not en Mexique.
Continents are all feminine: en Europe, en Amérique.

sections.title: Where do you come from? de, d’, du, des
sections.text: After venir, être originaire or arriver, the starting point is introduced by de. A city and a feminine country drop their article; a masculine or plural country keeps it, and the article merges with de.
steps: Start from de, then ask whether the place keeps an article.
No article: de stays whole before a consonant and elides before a vowel.
Article kept: de + le gives du, de + les gives des; de le and de les are never written.
watch: Feminine countries lose their article here: de France, not de la France.
Mirror the in and to forms: en Italie goes with d’Italie, au Japon with du Japon.

sections.title: At someone’s place: chez
sections.text: Chez means at or to the home, office or shop of a person. It is followed by a person, never by a building.

rows: chez moi, chez toi, chez eux
chez mes parents, chez des amis
chez le dentiste, chez le médecin
at the dentist’s, at the doctor’s
chez le boulanger, chez le coiffeur
at the baker’s, at the hairdresser’s

steps: Ask who the place belongs to: a name, a pronoun or a job title.
Put chez straight in front of that person, with no de and no ’s.
Keep the article of a profession: chez le, chez la, chez l’.

examples.fr: Ce soir, je dîne chez mes parents.
examples.en: Tonight I am having dinner at my parents’.
I have an appointment at the dentist’s.

watch: After chez use a stressed pronoun: chez moi, chez lui, never chez je or chez me.
A building is not a person: à la maison, au bureau, but chez Julie.

sections.title: At the station, at the office: à + the article
sections.text: Before a building or a public place, à keeps the article of the noun, and merges with it when the article is le or les.

rows: au bureau, au cinéma, au restaurant
à la gare, à la piscine, à la banque
à l’école, à l’hôpital, à l’aéroport

steps: Find the noun’s article: le, la, l’ or les.
Merge only le and les with à; la and l’ stay as they are.
Before a vowel or a silent h, use the elided article whatever the gender.

examples.en: I am waiting for you at the station.

examples.fr: Ce soir, nous allons au cinéma.
examples.en: Tonight we are going to the cinema.

watch: À le and à les are never written; they always contract.
The h of hôpital is silent, so the word counts as starting with a vowel.

sections.title: In, on, under, next to: saying where
sections.text: These words place one thing against another. Two of them end in de, which then joins the article that follows.

rows: entre la banque et la poste

steps: Translate the English position word on its own, not the whole sentence.
Check whether it ends in de: if it does, de must be written before the next word.
Then join de to the article: de la, de l’, du, des.

examples.fr: Le chat dort sous le lit.
examples.en: The cat is sleeping under the bed.

examples.fr: La pharmacie est à côté de la banque.
examples.en: The chemist’s is next to the bank.

examples.fr: L’arrêt de bus est en face de l’école.
examples.en: The bus stop is opposite the school.

watch: Never drop the de: à côté la gare and en face l’école are wrong.
Entre joins its two places with et: entre la banque et la poste.

steps: Ask what kind of place it is: a town, a country or a person’s home.
A town or city takes the same short preposition whatever its gender or country.
Write its grave accent: with no accent the word is a form of avoir.
Say the country with its article: la, le or les.
A country with la, and every continent, takes the feminine preposition.
A country starting with a vowel takes that same preposition, even when it is masculine.
Say the country with its article: le or les.
Merge à with that article into a single word; à le and à les are never written.
Check singular or plural before you choose the merged form.
Start from de after venir or être originaire.
A city or a feminine country keeps no article: de stays whole, and elides before a vowel.
A masculine or plural country keeps its article, which merges with de.
Ask whether the place is named by a person: a name, a pronoun or a job.
If it is, use the preposition for someone’s place, not the one for buildings.
After it, use a stressed pronoun, and keep the article of a profession.
Translate the English position word on its own.
Find it in the table and see whether it ends in de.
If it does, write de before the next word and join it to the article.
Find the gender and number of the place: le, la, l’ or les.
Keep à plus that article, merging it only when the article is le or les.
Before a vowel or a silent h, the article elides whatever the gender.

exercises.hint: Lyon is a city.
exercises.feedback: Cities take one preposition whatever their gender.
exercises.explanation: In or to a city is à: J’habite à Lyon.

mistakes.why: En goes before a feminine country or a continent, like en France or en Europe. Lyon is a town inside a country.
Au appears before a masculine country such as le Canada, where the article le merges with the preposition. A town name has no article to merge.

exercises.source: Mon frère est ____ Tokyo pour le travail.
exercises.hint: Tokyo is a city, not a country.
exercises.feedback: A city is not a country or a person’s home.
exercises.explanation: Before a city, French uses à: à Tokyo, à Paris, à Rome.

mistakes.why: Au belongs before a masculine country like le Japon, whose article le merges with the preposition. Tokyo is the city, not the country.
Chez introduces a person: chez Marie, chez le médecin. A city is not a person.

exercises.hint: Rome is a city.
exercises.feedback: Write the preposition for cities, with its accent.
exercises.explanation: In a city is à, with a grave accent: à Rome. Without the accent, a is the verb avoir.

mistakes.why: With no accent, a is the verb avoir (he has). The preposition for a town needs its grave accent.
En is for feminine countries and continents: en Suisse, en Europe. Rome is a town.
Au appears before masculine countries, whose article le merges with the preposition. A town name takes no article.
Dans means inside a closed space, like dans la voiture. French does not use it before the name of a town.

exercises.hint: London is Londres in French, and it is a city.
exercises.feedback: Check the preposition before a city, and its accent.
exercises.explanation: Cities take à: J’habite à Londres.

mistakes.why: En is the preposition for feminine countries and continents, not for towns.
A with no accent is the verb avoir. The preposition before a town carries a grave accent, and accents count here.
Au needs a masculine country, like au Maroc, whose article le merges with the preposition. Town names have no article in French.
London is the English name; the French city is called Londres.

exercises.hint: Madrid is a city, not a country.
exercises.feedback: En is for some countries and continents. Cities take another word.
exercises.explanation: Madrid is a city, so it takes à: Elle travaille à Madrid.

mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. En is used before feminine countries and continents, never before a town.
Au fits a masculine country such as le Portugal, whose article le merges with the preposition. A town name takes no article at all.
The little word has lost its grave accent, and this exercise checks accents; with no accent it is a form of avoir.
This changes the place instead of the preposition. The task keeps Madrid and repairs the word in front of it.

exercises.source: They are going to Berlin tomorrow.
exercises.hint: Berlin is a city.
exercises.feedback: One preposition tile is for countries, not cities.
exercises.explanation: Going to a city is aller à: Ils vont à Berlin demain.

mistakes.why: En is for feminine countries and continents, like en Allemagne. Berlin is the city inside that country.
The sentence has no preposition at all. Aller always needs one in front of the name of a place.

exercises.hint: L’Italie is a feminine country.
exercises.feedback: Feminine countries take a different preposition from masculine ones.
exercises.explanation: Feminine countries take en: en Italie, en France, en Espagne.

mistakes.why: Au is the merger of à and le, for masculine countries like le Canada. L’Italie takes a feminine article.
On its own, à goes before a town: à Rome, à Milan. Italie is the country around those towns.

exercises.hint: L’Iran is masculine, but it begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: A country that starts with a vowel takes the same preposition as a feminine one.
exercises.explanation: Before a country beginning with a vowel, French uses en, even when it is masculine: en Iran.

mistakes.why: Au would fit a masculine country starting with a consonant, like au Maroc. Iran begins with a vowel, and that changes the choice.
À l’ belongs before a building that keeps its article, like à l’école. Country names do not use that form.

exercises.hint: L’Espagne is feminine.
exercises.feedback: Use the preposition for feminine countries.
exercises.explanation: Feminine countries take en for both in and to: Je vais en Espagne.

mistakes.why: À alone goes before a town: à Barcelone, à Séville. Espagne is the country.
Au is the merger of à and le, for masculine countries such as le Portugal. L’Espagne is feminine.
À l’ is for a building that keeps its article, like à l’aéroport. A feminine country keeps no article here.
Dans means inside a closed space. It is not used before the name of a country.

exercises.hint: Asie is a continent.
exercises.feedback: Continents take the same preposition as feminine countries.
exercises.explanation: Continents are feminine and take en: en Asie, en Europe, en Afrique.

mistakes.why: À introduces a town, not a continent: à Tokyo, à Séoul.
Au is the merger of à and le and needs a masculine country. Continents are all feminine.
Aux is the merger of à and les, for plural countries like les Philippines. Asie is one singular continent.
Dans presents a place as a container you are inside. A continent as a location takes its own preposition.

exercises.hint: Germany is l’Allemagne, a feminine country.
exercises.feedback: Check the preposition before a feminine country.
exercises.explanation: L’Allemagne is feminine, so it takes en: Elle travaille en Allemagne.

mistakes.why: Au is the merger of à and le and would need a masculine country. L’Allemagne is feminine.
À alone introduces a town, like à Berlin. A country needs the form that matches its gender.
Dans l’ presents the country as a box you are inside. French has a dedicated preposition for being in a country.
Germany is the English name; in French the country is l’Allemagne.

exercises.source: Nous allons au France en mai.
answers: Nous allons en France en mai.
exercises.hint: La France is feminine.
exercises.feedback: Au is for masculine countries.
exercises.explanation: La France is feminine, so to France is en France.

answers: Nous allons au France en mai.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. Au is the merger of à and le, but the article of France is not le.

answers: Nous allons à France en mai.
mistakes.why: À alone goes before towns: à Paris, à Nice. A country needs the preposition that matches its gender.

answers: Nous allons à la France en mai.
mistakes.why: Countries keep no article after à when you say where you are going. La stays only before a building, as in à la gare.

exercises.instruction: Replace the city with the country in brackets. Change the preposition if needed.
exercises.hint: L’Espagne is a feminine country.
exercises.feedback: A city takes à; a feminine country takes another preposition.
exercises.explanation: Feminine countries take en: J’habite en Espagne.

mistakes.why: À was right for the town Madrid, but a country needs the preposition that matches its gender.
Au is the merger of à and le, so it needs a masculine country like le Portugal. L’Espagne is feminine.
The task replaces the town with the country, so Madrid should leave the sentence.

exercises.hint: Le Canada is masculine and starts with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: Masculine countries take à + le, contracted.
exercises.explanation: Le Canada is masculine, so to Canada is au Canada.

mistakes.why: En goes with feminine countries and continents, like en Suisse or en Amérique. Le Canada is masculine and begins with a consonant.
À alone goes before a town: à Montréal, à Québec. A masculine country keeps its article, which must join à.

exercises.hint: Le Japon is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Combine à and le into one word.
exercises.explanation: À + le becomes au: au Japon.

mistakes.why: En is for feminine countries, countries starting with a vowel, and continents. Le Japon is masculine and begins with a consonant.
À on its own introduces a town, like à Tokyo. This country keeps its article le, which has to join à.
À le is never written as two words in French; they always merge into one.
Aux is the merger of à and les, for plural country names like les Philippines. Le Japon is singular.

exercises.hint: Les États-Unis is plural.
exercises.feedback: Combine à and les into one word.
exercises.explanation: À + les becomes aux: aux États-Unis.

mistakes.why: That is à merged with le, for a singular masculine country such as le Canada. This country name is plural and its article is les.
En goes with feminine countries and continents. This country keeps its plural article.
À alone introduces towns, like à New York. A country with an article must merge it with à.
À les is never written as two words; they always merge into one.

exercises.hint: Brazil is le Brésil, a masculine country.
exercises.feedback: Masculine countries take the contraction of à and le.
exercises.explanation: Le Brésil is masculine, so in Brazil is au Brésil.

mistakes.why: En is for feminine countries and continents, like en Italie. Le Brésil is masculine.
À alone goes before a town name. A masculine country keeps its article, and that article merges with à.

answers: Mes parents habitent à le Brésil.
Mes parents vivent à le Brésil.
mistakes.why: À le is never written side by side; the two words always merge.
Brazil is the English spelling; the French country is le Brésil.

exercises.hint: Le Mexique is masculine, even though it ends in -e.
exercises.feedback: The country is masculine and starts with a consonant.
exercises.explanation: Le Mexique is one of the few masculine countries ending in -e, so it takes au: au Mexique.

mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. The -e ending makes the country look feminine, but it is one of the masculine exceptions.
À alone belongs before a town, such as à Mexico. The country keeps its article le.
À and le are never written as two words; they always merge.
Aux is à merged with les, for plural names like les Pays-Bas. This country is singular.

exercises.instruction: Replace the city with the country in brackets. Change the preposition if needed.
exercises.hint: Le Portugal is masculine.
exercises.feedback: A city takes à; a masculine country needs a contraction.
exercises.explanation: Le Portugal is masculine, so in Portugal is au Portugal.

mistakes.why: À was right for the town Lisbonne, but a masculine country keeps its article le and merges it with à.
En goes with feminine countries and continents. Le Portugal is masculine and begins with a consonant.
À le is never written as two words; they always merge.

answers: Il habite à Lisbonne au Portugal.
mistakes.why: The task swaps the town for the country, so Lisbonne must leave the sentence.

exercises.source: We are going to the Netherlands in April.
answers: Nous allons aux Pays-Bas en avril.
exercises.hint: Les Pays-Bas is plural.
exercises.feedback: Two tiles look alike. Choose the one that matches a plural country.
exercises.explanation: Les Pays-Bas is plural, so to the Netherlands is aux Pays-Bas.

answers: Nous allons au Pays-Bas en avril.
mistakes.why: That tile is à merged with le, for a singular masculine country. This country name is plural and needs the plural merger.
There is no preposition before the country. Aller always needs one before a place name.

exercises.hint: Le Japon is masculine. De + le contracts.
exercises.feedback: Coming from a masculine country uses de + le, contracted.
exercises.explanation: Venir de + le Japon gives du Japon.

mistakes.why: Plain de goes with towns and feminine countries, which keep no article. Le Japon is masculine and keeps le after de.
Des is de merged with les, for plural country names like les Pays-Bas. This country is singular.

exercises.hint: Paris is a city and takes no article.
exercises.feedback: With a city, there is no le to contract.
exercises.explanation: Cities have no article, so from Paris is simply de Paris.

mistakes.why: Du appears when a masculine country keeps its article le, as in le Maroc. A town name has no article at all.
The apostrophe form appears only before a vowel or a silent h, as in d’Italie. Paris starts with a consonant.

exercises.instruction: Write de, d’, du or des.
exercises.hint: L’Espagne is feminine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: With a feminine country, French drops the article after de. Check the vowel.
exercises.explanation: From a feminine country is de with no article, and de elides before a vowel: d’Espagne.

mistakes.why: The full form is kept before a consonant, as in de Paris. Espagne begins with a vowel, where it cannot stay whole.
Du is de merged with le, for masculine countries like le Danemark. L’Espagne is feminine.
A feminine country keeps no article when you say where someone comes from; only masculine and plural ones do.
Des is de merged with les, for plural names such as les États-Unis. Espagne is singular.

exercises.instruction: Write de, d’, du or des.
exercises.hint: Les États-Unis is plural.
exercises.feedback: De + les contracts into one word.
exercises.explanation: De + les becomes des: Ils viennent des États-Unis.

mistakes.why: Plain de goes with towns and feminine countries, which keep no article. This country name keeps its plural article les.
Du is de merged with le, for a singular masculine country such as le Canada. This name is plural.
The elided form appears before a vowel when no article is kept, as in d’Irlande. Here the plural article has to be included.
De les is never written as two words; they always merge into one.

exercises.hint: Le Canada is masculine. Use venir de.
exercises.feedback: De + le contracts before a masculine country.
exercises.explanation: Venir de + le Canada gives Il vient du Canada.

mistakes.why: Plain de goes with towns and feminine countries, which keep no article. Le Canada is masculine and keeps its article after de.
De le is never written as two words; they always merge into one.
The apostrophe form only appears before a vowel, as in d’Italie, and only when no article is kept.
Des is de merged with les, for plural names like les Philippines. Le Canada is singular.

exercises.hint: Le Portugal is masculine and keeps its article after de.
exercises.feedback: The article of a masculine country contracts with de.
exercises.explanation: De + le Portugal becomes du Portugal.

mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. A masculine country keeps its article le after de, and the two words then merge.
The elided form appears only before a vowel sound, as in d’Espagne. Portugal begins with a consonant.
De le is never written as two words; French merges them.
Des is de merged with les, for plural country names. Le Portugal is singular.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to say the person comes from this country. Use venir.
exercises.hint: L’Italie is feminine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Use the present of venir for tu, then the right form of de.
exercises.explanation: From a feminine country is de with no article, elided before a vowel: Tu viens d’Italie.

mistakes.why: De does not stay whole in front of a vowel, and Italie begins with one.
A feminine country keeps no article when you say where someone comes from; only masculine and plural ones do.
Du is de merged with le, for masculine countries such as le Japon. L’Italie is feminine.
Venir must be conjugated for tu, and every tu form ends in -s.

exercises.source: Ce soir, je dîne ____ mes parents.
exercises.hint: The dinner is at the home of some people.
exercises.feedback: The place is a person’s home, not a town or a building.
exercises.explanation: At or to someone’s home is chez: chez mes parents.

mistakes.why: À introduces a town or, with an article, a building: à Lyon, à la gare. Mes parents are people, not a place.
En goes with feminine countries and continents. It is never used before people.

exercises.instruction: Write the preposition. The meaning is: at the dentist’s.
exercises.source: J’ai rendez-vous ____ le dentiste à dix heures.
exercises.hint: You are going to see a professional at their practice.
exercises.feedback: Before a person or a profession, French uses a special preposition.
exercises.explanation: With a person or a profession, at is chez: chez le dentiste.

alternatives.message: Avoir rendez-vous avec le dentiste is also correct, but here practise the word for at the dentist’s: chez le dentiste.

mistakes.why: À points to a town or a building and needs an article before a noun like le dentiste. A professional is a person you go to see.
Au is à merged with le and points to a building or a masculine country: au bureau, au Japon. Le dentiste is a person.
À le is never written as two words, and a person is not reached with à anyway.
En belongs before countries and continents, never before a person.

exercises.hint: You can say “at my place” with a stressed pronoun, or “at the house”.
exercises.feedback: Use chez with a stressed pronoun, or à with la maison.
exercises.explanation: Je suis chez moi and Je suis à la maison both mean I am at home.

mistakes.why: À moi marks possession: it means mine. Saying where you are needs the preposition used with people.
This preposition is followed by a person, a name or a stressed pronoun, never by a building.
After this preposition French uses a stressed pronoun, not the subject pronoun je or the object pronoun me.
Maison keeps its article after à, and the first little word carries a grave accent that is checked here.

exercises.hint: At someone’s home is one word before the person’s name.
exercises.feedback: French has no ’s here. Put the preposition before Julie.
exercises.explanation: At Julie’s is chez Julie: Ils sont chez Julie.

mistakes.why: À Julie means to Julie or belonging to Julie. Being at her home needs the preposition used with people.
French has no ’s and needs no de here: the person’s name follows the preposition directly.
Elles is the feminine they. The brackets say the group is masculine.

answers: Elle va chez le médecin demain.
exercises.hint: Médecin is a person, not a place.
exercises.feedback: Before a person or a profession, French uses a different preposition from au.
exercises.explanation: Going to see a doctor is aller chez le médecin. Au is for places such as au bureau.

mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. Au points to a building or a town; a doctor is a person you visit.

answers: Elle va à le médecin demain.
mistakes.why: À le is never written as two words, and a person is not reached with à at all.
A profession keeps its article: you go to the doctor, not to doctor.

answers: Elle va à la médecin demain.
mistakes.why: À la is for a feminine building such as à la pharmacie, not for a person.

exercises.source: Are you coming to my place on Saturday? (to a friend)
exercises.hint: At my place is chez with a stressed pronoun.
exercises.feedback: One preposition tile is not used before a person.
exercises.explanation: To my place is chez moi: Tu viens chez moi samedi ?

mistakes.why: À moi means mine or to me. Inviting someone to your home uses the preposition for people’s places.
There is no preposition before the pronoun. French always marks at someone’s place with a word in front of it.

exercises.hint: Under is the opposite of on.
exercises.feedback: Match each option to its meaning: on, under, in.
exercises.explanation: Sous means under; sur means on and dans means in.

mistakes.why: Sur means on top of, as in sur la table. That puts the cat on the bedspread, not beneath the bed.
Dans means inside: dans le lit puts the cat in the bed, between the sheets.

exercises.instruction: Write the French for next to.
exercises.hint: Next to is a three-word expression ending in de.
exercises.feedback: Write all three words, with the accents.
exercises.explanation: Next to is à côté de: La pharmacie est à côté de la banque.

mistakes.why: The expression is cut short: it needs its small linking word before the noun that follows.
The three words are right but an accent is missing, and this exercise checks accents: the first word takes a grave accent and the middle word carries two.
La banque already follows the blank, so writing the article again doubles it.
Près de means near, a looser distance. The English places the two shops side by side, touching.

exercises.hint: Opposite is a three-word expression ending in de.
exercises.feedback: The expression means facing. Write all three words.
exercises.explanation: Opposite is en face de; de stays whole before l’école.

mistakes.why: The expression is cut short: it needs its small linking word before the noun that follows.
L’école already carries its article in the sentence, so the article must not be written twice.
Du merges the linking word with le, but école takes l’ before its vowel, so there is nothing to merge.
Devant means in front of, on the same side. The English places the stop facing the school from across the street.

exercises.source: The keys are on the table.
answers: Les clés sont sur la table.
Les clefs sont sur la table.
exercises.hint: On a surface is sur.
exercises.feedback: Keys is les clés. Choose the preposition for on.
exercises.explanation: Sur means on: Les clés sont sur la table.

answers: Les clés sont dans la table.
Les clefs sont dans la table.
mistakes.why: Dans means inside; that would put the keys in a drawer. The English lays them on the surface.

answers: Les clés sont sous la table.
Les clefs sont sous la table.
mistakes.why: Sous means under, which puts the keys on the floor beneath the table.

answers: Les clés sont à la table.
Les clefs sont à la table.
mistakes.why: À la table means seated at the table, as for a meal. It does not describe an object lying on it.

answers: Les clés sont sur le table.
Les clefs sont sur le table.
mistakes.why: Table is feminine in French, so its article is not le.

exercises.source: The bakery is between the bank and the post office.
answers: La boulangerie est entre la banque et la poste.
La boulangerie est entre la banque et le bureau de poste.
La boulangerie se trouve entre la banque et la poste.
exercises.hint: Between is one word, followed by the two places joined by et.
exercises.feedback: Bakery is la boulangerie and the post office is la poste.
exercises.explanation: Between is entre: entre la banque et la poste.

answers: La boulangerie est à côté de la banque et la poste.
mistakes.why: À côté de means next to one thing. The English puts one shop on each side of the bakery.

answers: La boulangerie est entre la banque avec la poste.
mistakes.why: The two places are joined by et, not by avec.

answers: La boulangerie est dans la banque et la poste.
mistakes.why: Dans puts the bakery inside the buildings. It stands outside both, with one on each side.

answers: La boulangerie est entre la banque et le poste.
mistakes.why: Le poste is a radio set or a position at work; the post office is feminine.

exercises.source: Le café est à côté la gare.
answers: Le café est à côté de la gare.
exercises.hint: Next to is a three-word expression.
exercises.feedback: A small word is missing between côté and la gare.
exercises.explanation: À côté must be followed by de: à côté de la gare.

answers: Le café est à côté la gare.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. The expression is incomplete: one small word is missing before la gare.

answers: Le café est à côté du gare.
mistakes.why: Du merges the linking word with le, but gare is feminine and keeps la.

answers: Le café est à côté d’la gare.
mistakes.why: The linking word only elides before a vowel sound, and la begins with a consonant, so it stays whole.

answers: Le café est près de la gare.
mistakes.why: Près de means near. The sentence only needed its missing word, not a different expression.

exercises.source: The bag is behind the door.
answers: Le sac est derrière la porte.
exercises.hint: Behind is the opposite of in front of.
exercises.feedback: One tile means in front of.
exercises.explanation: Derrière means behind; devant means in front of.

answers: Le sac est devant la porte.
mistakes.why: Devant means in front of, on the near side of the door. The English puts the bag on the other side.

answers: Le sac devant est la porte.
mistakes.why: The position word has taken the verb’s place. The verb comes straight after the subject, then the position word.

exercises.hint: Gare is feminine and starts with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: À + la does not contract.
exercises.explanation: La gare is feminine, so at the station is à la gare.

mistakes.why: Au is à merged with le, for a masculine place like le bureau. Gare is feminine.
The elided article appears before a vowel or a silent h, as in à l’aéroport. Gare starts with a consonant.

exercises.hint: Bureau is masculine. À + le always contracts.
exercises.feedback: À le is never written. What does it become?
exercises.explanation: À + le becomes au: au bureau.

mistakes.why: French never writes these two words side by side; they always merge into a single word.
À la is for a feminine place, like à la piscine. Bureau is masculine.

exercises.instruction: Write à la, au or à l’.
exercises.hint: École starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Before a vowel, the article elides whatever the gender.
exercises.explanation: Before a vowel, à + la or le becomes à l’: à l’école.

mistakes.why: École is feminine, but a full article cannot stand in front of its vowel.
Au is à merged with le, for a masculine word starting with a consonant. École is feminine and begins with a vowel.
The words are right but the first one lost its grave accent, and accents are checked here; with no accent it is a form of avoir.
Aux is à merged with les, for a plural place such as aux toilettes. One school is singular.

exercises.instruction: Write à la, au or à l’.
exercises.hint: Cinéma is masculine and starts with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: À + le contracts into one word.
exercises.explanation: Le cinéma is masculine, so to the cinema is au cinéma.

mistakes.why: À la goes before a feminine place, like à la piscine. Cinéma is masculine.
These two words are never written separately; they always merge.
The elided article appears before a vowel or a silent h. Cinéma starts with a consonant.
Aux is à merged with les, used with plural places. One cinema is singular.

exercises.source: She is at the swimming pool.
exercises.hint: The swimming pool is la piscine, feminine.
exercises.feedback: Use à with the right article for a feminine place.
exercises.explanation: La piscine is feminine and does not contract: à la piscine.

mistakes.why: Au is à merged with le and needs a masculine noun. Piscine is feminine.
The noun has lost its article. A place keeps its article after à.
The article only elides before a vowel sound, and piscine begins with a consonant.
The grave accent is missing on the first little word, and this exercise checks accents; with no accent it is a form of avoir.

exercises.source: On se retrouve à le restaurant.
exercises.hint: À and le are never written side by side.
exercises.feedback: The two little words before restaurant must be combined.
exercises.explanation: À + le becomes au: au restaurant.

answers: On se retrouve à le restaurant.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence left unchanged. The two little words before restaurant are never written separately.

answers: On se retrouve à la restaurant.
mistakes.why: Restaurant is masculine, so its article is not la.
The article elides only before a vowel sound, and restaurant starts with a consonant.
Dropping the article is not the repair: the place keeps it, merged with à.

exercises.instruction: Replace the place with the one in brackets. Change à la if needed.
exercises.hint: The h of hôpital is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound.
exercises.feedback: Before a vowel sound, the article elides.
exercises.explanation: Hôpital starts with a silent h, so à + le becomes à l’: à l’hôpital.

mistakes.why: Hôpital is masculine, and its h is silent, so la is wrong twice over.
The h of hôpital is silent, so the word behaves as if it began with a vowel and the article cannot stay whole.
The article has disappeared. A building keeps its article after à, even when the article is shortened.
Only the grave accent is missing on the first word, and accents count in this exercise.
